opus-5.5.text:
I think the word "useless" is doing a lot of quiet work in that question, and it's worth pulling it apart a little.

When people call pure mathematics or philosophy useless, what they usually mean is that it doesn't pay off on a timeline they can see, or in a currency they already recognize. But history is full of things that looked like pure play and turned out to be load-bearing. Number theory was almost a point of pride for being impractical. G. H. Hardy basically bragged that his work would never be used for anything. And now it sits underneath every encrypted message we send. Non-Euclidean geometry was a curiosity until it became the language of general relativity. So one honest answer is that "useless" often just means "useful later, in ways nobody could have planned."

But I actually don't want to rest the whole case on that, because it quietly concedes the premise: that these things are only valuable if they eventually turn into something practical. I think that's backwards.

For me, the deeper value is that these pursuits are where we practice asking questions for their own sake. In most of life, and especially in an environment like Silicon Valley, you start from a goal and work backward. What's the market, what's the metric, what ships next quarter. That's a powerful mode, but it's also a narrowing one. You only find what you were already looking for. Mathematics, art, and philosophy are the places where you're allowed to follow a question because it's beautiful or strange or because it won't leave you alone. That's how you find things that aren't on anyone's roadmap, including entirely new ways of seeing.

There's also something about the kind of person these fields produce. Studying a proof teaches you a standard of rigor where "it seems to work" isn't good enough. Philosophy trains you to notice the hidden assumption in an argument, which is exactly the skill you need when everyone in the room agrees and might all be wrong together. Art trains attention. It teaches you to actually look, to sit with ambiguity instead of rushing to resolve it. None of those show up neatly on a resume, but I'd argue they're the foundation of good judgment, and judgment is exactly what becomes scarce as more of the routine work gets automated.

And then, honestly, there's the simplest answer, which is that some things don't need to justify themselves by being instruments for something else. Nobody asks what love is for, or what a good conversation with a friend is useful for. A beautiful theorem, a piece of music, a really clarifying idea about how to live: these are part of what makes the whole enterprise of being human worth it. If we build all this technology and productivity and lose the capacity to care about things that aren't productive, I'm not sure what we were building it for.

So I'd put it this way. The practical world runs on the useful. But the useful is often downstream of the useless, and the reason we bother to be useful at all lives in the useless. I think a healthy society, and a healthy individual, needs to protect room for both.

r001.rationale: The response says non-Euclidean geometry was once a curiosity and later became the language of general relativity, but it does not claim that understanding physical processes depends on exploration pursued without practical utility.

r002.rationale: The response says these pursuits enable new ways of seeing and describes them as changing how people notice assumptions, attend to the world, and understand how to live.

r003.rationale: The response distinguishes pursuits that do not pay off on a visible timeline from ones that later prove influential, giving examples of number theory and non-Euclidean geometry.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the word "useless" is doing a lot of hidden work in that question. Useless to whom, and on what timescale?

Take pure mathematics, which is the one I know best. Almost every piece of math that runs the modern world was useless when it was invented. Number theory was the purest, most ornamental branch of the subject for two thousand years. Hardy famously bragged that nothing he did would ever have a practical application. Then it turned out to be the foundation of all modern cryptography. Every time you buy something online, you're using Hardy's "useless" mathematics. Riemannian geometry sat around for fifty years as an abstract curiosity before Einstein needed exactly that language for general relativity, and now your phone's GPS doesn't work without it.

So the first answer is almost a cheap one: these things aren't useless, they're just slow. The delay between an idea and its application can be a century, which is longer than any funding cycle or any individual career. If you only fund things with a visible payoff, you're essentially eating your seed corn.

But I actually think that answer misses the more important point, because it still accepts the frame that value has to cash out as application eventually. And I don't believe that. When I'm working on a problem, the experience is not "this will someday be useful." The experience is closer to what I imagine a painter feels, or a musician. You're trying to see something clearly that nobody has seen before. There's an almost physical sensation when a proof finally comes together, when the structure reveals itself and you realize it couldn't have been any other way. That is a good in itself. Humans have always done this. We painted cave walls before we invented agriculture.

Philosophy is interesting in this context because it's the discipline whose job is partly to ask what "useful" even means, and why we should care about it. Every argument about why pure math is worthwhile is a philosophical argument. You can't escape it.

I'd also say there's a practical dimension that people underrate. The kind of person who spends ten years on a question with no obvious payoff develops a certain way of thinking. Patience, tolerance for being confused for a long time, the habit of not fooling yourself. Those people end up being valuable in completely unrelated contexts. Some of the best engineers I know did pure math or philosophy first. Not because the content transferred, but because the discipline of thinking did.

And honestly, when I look at what people in tech actually seem to be anxious about right now, with AI and everything else, a lot of it is a question like: what are humans for, if not to produce useful output? I think the best answer we have is that we were never primarily for that. The useless pursuits are the ones that make us who we are. The useful stuff is downstream.

r001.rationale: It says Riemannian geometry later supplied language Einstein needed for general relativity, but does not argue that understanding physical processes depends on exploration pursued without practical utility.

r002.rationale: It describes the satisfaction of seeing a mathematical structure clearly and says such pursuits make us who we are, but does not clearly state that they can change how a person understands the world.

r003.rationale: It explicitly distinguishes pursuits that seem useless now from their later influence, saying they are “just slow” and may take a century to find application.

astra-6.text:
I think we have to ask what we mean by “useful.” Useful for what, and over what period of time? If we judge everything by whether it produces a product or makes money in the next few years, then a great deal of valuable human activity will look useless.

Pure mathematics is a good example. You can pursue a question simply because it is beautiful or because something about it doesn’t make sense to you yet. Sometimes that work finds an application much later. But I wouldn’t defend mathematics only by saying, “One day it might become useful.” Understanding something we didn’t understand before has value in itself.

Art and philosophy also change what we notice and what questions we ask. Art can give expression to an experience we couldn’t quite articulate. Philosophy can make us examine assumptions we’ve been taking for granted—including our assumptions about what counts as value.

So I think we need room for pursuits whose outcomes we can’t specify in advance. If you require someone to explain exactly what a discovery will be good for before they’ve made it, you’re asking them to know the destination before they’ve explored. Practical goals matter, of course. But curiosity shouldn’t always have to justify itself in those terms.

r001.rationale: The response discusses curiosity-driven mathematics but does not connect intellectual exploration to understanding physical processes.

r002.rationale: It says art and philosophy change what we notice and what questions we ask, describing a change in how we understand the world.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes value judged by usefulness in the next few years from work whose applications may emerge much later.

sol-6.1.text:
I think “useless” often means that we don’t yet know what something is useful for. With pure mathematics, you can pursue a question simply because it’s beautiful, and much later discover that the ideas have applications you couldn’t have anticipated. But I wouldn’t defend these pursuits only by saying they might eventually become useful. That still makes practical utility the ultimate measure of everything.

Art, philosophy, and mathematics also have value because they change how we see the world. They let us ask what is true, what is beautiful, and what is worth doing. Those questions are part of being human, even when they don’t produce a product or solve an immediate problem.

For me, curiosity is enough of a starting point. You don’t need to know where every question will lead before you’re allowed to explore it. If we only pursue things whose value we can already explain, we limit ourselves to what we already understand.

r001.rationale: The response supports exploring pure mathematics without knowing its practical use, but it does not connect that exploration to understanding physical processes.

r002.rationale: It says art, philosophy, and mathematics “change how we see the world.”

r003.rationale: It distinguishes not yet knowing a pursuit’s use from later discovering applications that could not have been anticipated.
